I'm Gurleen, and looking back at Class 10, I think that was the year I started asking why.
Our school rule said girls must wear two plaits with black ribbons. Boys had no hair rule at all. One morning in assembly line, Ms Shalini told me to redo my single plait. I asked, “Ma'am, who made this rule, and why only for girls?”
The line went dead silent. A few girls stared at their shoes. My friend Harleen whispered, “Are you mad?”
Ms Shalini said, “Don't argue, just do it.” My mother, later, called it attitude.
But I wasn't trying to be rude. I truly wanted to know. That week I read the school diary and found the rule was from 1987. Nobody I asked could explain it.

qa.q: What colour ribbons did the rule say girls must wear?
qa.a: Black ribbons.

qa.a: Gurleen felt misunderstood and frustrated, because the question came from real curiosity, not a wish to be rude.

qa.a: Gurleen could ask for a quiet time with the teacher or write to the principal, sharing the rule's date and asking for its reason.

qa.q: How might Harleen have felt in that silent line?
qa.a: Harleen was probably nervous and a bit shocked, worried Gurleen would get into trouble, which is why Harleen whispered.

grounding: A teenager recalls starting to ask why a rule exists and who made it, which adults read as defiance though it was honest questioning.

The room murmured. Nobody raised a hand.
Pooja stood up. Her knees were shaking. “Ma'am, I understand we need to be safe. But I don't think this is fair for those of us who need the town library for projects. Can we talk about it?”
